rv.q: Izzard isn't soaring to the text's dizzying heights or dropping to its gutting psychophysical depths: She's making her way steadily through.

Izzard offering distinctive spins on every member of the court of Elsinore, popping in and out of them and breezily performing scenes opposite herself, much as she always has in her stand-up — and with results that are often as funny.
Izzard is lucid and moving through that soliloquy and the others, during which Hamlet, when not considering suicide, often chastises himself for his inability to act on revenging his father's murder.
But Izzard's initial energy proves unsustainable over the course of five acts (adapter Mark Izzard cuts down Shakespeare’s text into two, but the meat of all five remains).
Izzard unfortunately fails to plumb the full pathos of the two key female figures.
This adaptation lacks an animating point of view beyond the stunt of having a single actor play all the roles.

cn.t: Critics are divided on Izzard's solo Hamlet, with reactions ranging from underwhelmed to enthusiastic. While some find the multi-character performance less distinctive than her Great Expectations, others praise her ability to bring Shakespeare's text to vivid life.
